query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a Mo-based refractory alloy interlayer between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr will improve interfacial integrity under fusion reactor conditions by accommodating thermal expansion differences and mitigating deleterious chemical reactions.
generation.material_initial_state: Tungsten (W) and CuCrZr are directly bonded, but due to their large mismatch in coefficients of thermal expansion and chemical reactivity at high temperatures, the interface is prone to cracking, intermetallic formation, and delamination under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin, composition-optimized Mo-based refractory alloy as an interlayer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, high-heat-flux, and irradiation environments simulating operational conditions in nuclear fusion reactors.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo-based interlayer, with an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and inert chemical behavior, acts as a graded interface that absorbs thermal stresses and prevents deleterious interfacial reactions.
generation.mechanism: By adjusting the chemical composition to yield an intermediate thermal expansion and chemical inertness, the Mo-based interlayer reduces the mismatch-induced stresses and suppresses the formation of brittle phases at the interface, thereby ensuring structural integrity under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The interlayered system will exhibit improved bonding strength, reduced interfacial cracking/delamination, and enhanced durability compared to a direct W/CuCrZr bond under fusion reactor service conditions.
generation.baseline: Direct bonding of tungsten to CuCrZr, which suffers from significant thermal stress and interfacial degradation during extreme thermal cycling and irradiation.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected within the thermal load, temperature, and radiation regimes typical for fusion reactor divertor applications; performance outside these limits remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: While theory and intermediate material design principles support the use of a Mo-based alloy, the exact alloy composition and long-term behavior under neutron irradiation and cyclic thermal loading require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bi-layer samples: one with a direct W to CuCrZr bond and another with an interlayer of a Mo-based alloy. Subject both sets to simulated fusion reactor conditions including high thermal loads, rapid thermal cycling, and irradiation. Evaluate the interfacial bonding quality and microstructural integrity before and after exposure.
measurements: Observations of crack formation/delamination (using SEM or TEM)
Phase composition analysis at the interface (via XRD or EDS)
Thermal cycling performance and durability under simulated irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-based interlayer does not significantly reduce interfacial degradation (i.e., no statistically significant improvement in bonding strength or reduction in crack/delamination occurrences compared to the direct bond) under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
